passages.text: But let every door be opened to him, and let all the wretched, enacted laws be dissolved, laws laid down for jealous people. Dominated by folly and unwilling to understand what is reasonable, and also looking suspiciously at the so-called adulterers, these people are reasonably made sport of by Zeus himself through Minos and Rhadamanthys, by means of enacted laws. For Love cannot be restrained once he has taken up residence in souls. The passion of lovers is not voluntary. Indeed, Zeus himself, the lawgiver of these people, had relations with countless women. Some wise men praise him as a benefactor in childbearing, granting human beings union with himself. But among those whom he knew did not recognize the favor, he changed his appearance, so that he would neither distress them nor seem to act against the laws he himself had established. Therefore, for the sake of a good life, you must devote yourself to philosophy and imitate those acknowledged to be superior, whose unions have been countless.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The laws are instituted or laid down, contrasting humanly established prohibition with the speaker's account of irresistible love. Arbitrary is a possible evaluative reading, but enacted does not add that judgment to the adjective itself.

lexical_decisions.chosen: are reasonably made sport of ... by means of enacted laws
lexical_decisions.rationale: The passive verb describes the jealous people as being played with or mocked, not as themselves playing. The positive judgment reasonably is the letter writer's, and is not silently reversed to match the surrounding narrative's moral position.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: παρ’ οἷς δὲ ἐπὶ τῷ χάριτι ἠπίστατο ἀγνοούμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: among those whom he knew did not recognize the favor
lexical_decisions.rationale: The masculine passive participle refers to Zeus as unrecognized in respect of the favor. More literally, among those by whom he knew he was unrecognized for the favor. The rendering does not supply a specific husband or woman where the plural leaves the recipients general.

lexical_decisions.chosen: you must devote yourself to philosophy
lexical_decisions.rationale: The feminine participle addresses the female recipient. The main English does not need a gendered pronoun, but retains the instruction to attend to philosophy rather than treating philosophy as an external agent.

passages.text: And so as not to waste time needlessly on further proofs, I will begin with Zeus himself, the father of gods and humans, and disclose some of his unions; recalling them all is impossible because of their number. Listen, then, to the unions of great Zeus himself that were concealed through changes of form because of foolish men's jealousy. First, wishing to remove for the wise the supposed sin of adultery arising from different unions, when he was about to marry, and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people, he obtained a sinless marriage through the supposed sin, as I said. For he marries Hera, his own sister, having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo. From her Hebe and Eileithyia were born. For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone, just as Hera gives birth to Hephaestus.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The adjective can indicate differing or varied unions. The context presents the writer's attempt to remove the charge of adultery from multiple unions, but the phrase is not expanded to specify particular partners not named here.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: καὶ ὡς ἐπὶ πρώτῃ εὐνῇ κατὰ τοὺς πολλοὺς μοιχὸς εἰδὼς οὐ γινόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: and knowing that, as at a first bed, he was not becoming an adulterer according to most people
lexical_decisions.rationale: The unusual first-bed comparison and the appeal to most people's judgment are both preserved. Bed is a sexual or marital union here. The nominative participles are read as Zeus's knowledge of his own not becoming an adulterer; an alternative takes knowing and not becoming as parallel descriptions. The main text does not resolve the argument into an unstated rule about either partner's previous marital status.

lexical_decisions.chosen: having made himself resemble the plumage of a cuckoo
lexical_decisions.rationale: The dative literally names a cuckoo's feather or plumage. Plumage preserves that expressed image rather than simply replacing it with the whole bird; a cuckoo's feather is a narrower alternative.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: τὴν Μῆτιν γὰρ χωρὶς τῆς πρὸς τινὰ μίξεως ἀποκυΐσκει
lexical_decisions.chosen: For he gives birth to Metis without union with anyone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The active verb assigns the birth to Zeus. The supplied name and unusual parentage are retained rather than harmonized with other versions of the myth.

passages.text: He also has relations with a sister born to him from Uranus and Sea through Cronus's castration, .... Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone. He also has relations with Antiope, daughter of Nycteus, having made himself like a satyr; from her Amphion and Zethus were born. He unites with Alcmene, Amphitryon's wife, resembling Amphitryon her husband; from her Heracles was born. He also approaches Aegina, daughter of Asopus, becoming an eagle; from her Aeacus is born. He lies with Amalthea, daughter of Phocus, resembling a bear. He flowed down upon Danae, daughter of Acrisius, as gold; from her Perseus flew forth. For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas. He united with Europa, daughter of Phoenix, through a bull; from her Minos, Rhadamanthys, and Sarpedon sprang forth. With Eurymedusa, daughter of Achelous, he became an ant; from her came Myrmidon. With the nymph of Hersaeus he became a vulture; from her came the Palici in Sicily. He united with earth-born Himalia in Rhodes through rain; from her came Spartaeus, Cronius, and Cytus. He took Cassiopeia as a bride, resembling Phoenix her husband; from her Atymnius sprang forth for him. With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose and fathered Helen; and again, becoming a star, he brought forth Castor and Polydeuces. For Lamia he changed into a hoopoe.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The genitive can describe a castration associated with Cronus as agent or as the person castrated. Castration carried out by Cronus is a material alternative. The possessive English preserves the association without supplying an otherwise unnamed victim in this clause.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Ἔρως καὶ Κύπρις, ἣν καὶ Διδώνην λέγουσιν
lexical_decisions.chosen: Eros and Cypris, whom they also call Didone
lexical_decisions.rationale: The two names after the printed gap remain a fragment, without an invented verb or genealogical connection. The feminine relative refers to Cypris. Didone transliterates the printed name rather than silently correcting it to Dione.
The verb's flight image is retained. Sprang forth would be a more idiomatic birth expression but would conceal the explicit flying verb.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Καλλιστοῖ τῇ Λυκάονος ἠγριώθη λέων, καὶ ἄλλον τίκτει Ἀρκάδα
lexical_decisions.chosen: For Callisto, daughter of Lycaon, he became a fierce lion, and she bears another, Arcas
lexical_decisions.rationale: The supplied lion form and the word another are retained without harmonizing other accounts. The subject of bears is inferred as Callisto from the reproductive context; the masculine Arcas identifies the child.

The genitive relationship is left broad. Νύμφη can also mean bride or young wife, so bride of Hersaeus is a material alternative. The text is not expanded into a specific genealogy or a different familiar myth.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: Νεμέσει τῇ Θεστίου, τῇ καὶ Λήδᾳ νομισθείσῃ, κύκνος ἢ χὴν γενόμενος
lexical_decisions.chosen: With Nemesis, daughter of Thestius, who was also considered Leda, he became a swan or a goose
lexical_decisions.rationale: Both the alternative bird forms and the source's identification of Nemesis with Leda are preserved rather than choosing a single familiar version.

source_issues.issue: The selected edition prints a four-dot gap. The English retains exactly four dots and the following fragment Eros and Cypris, without inventing the lost connection or restoring a missing birth statement. The surviving passage is not represented as an unbroken original.

passages.text: Resembling a shepherd, he makes Mnemosyne the mother of the Muses. He marries Semele, daughter of Cadmus, while blazing, and from her brings forth Dionysus. He himself takes his daughter Persephone as a bride, having made himself like a serpent; she was also considered the wife of his brother Pluto. He has relations with many other women even without changing form, their husbands feeling no jealousy as though over a sin, but knowing well that by freely sharing in union with their wives he fathers children, granting them Hermeses, Apollos, Dionysuses, Endymions, and all the others we have mentioned, outstanding in beauty from union with him.

lexical_decisions.rationale: The participle describes Zeus as flaming or blazing. The translation does not supply a specific material body or explain the event using a different familiar account.

lexical_decisions.chosen: He himself takes his daughter Persephone as a bride
lexical_decisions.rationale: The verb can concern marrying off or taking in marriage. The reflexive emphasis and the sexual sequence favor Zeus himself as the participant taking his daughter as a bride; the alternative of his giving her in marriage remains lexically possible.

The source prints these names in the plural. The English preserves that conspicuous pattern rather than normalizing them to singular named children; it can characterize children of the named divine types.
The adverb may express abundance or the absence of jealousy or grudging. Freely keeps both generosity and lack of restraint available without adding the claim that every husband consented.

passages.text: So that I do not spend my time on an endless account, you will find ungrudging unions among all the gods along with Zeus—unions that foolish people call adulteries of the gods. They do not even avoid unions with males as shameful, but practice this too as something becoming. Thus Zeus himself loves Ganymede; Poseidon, Pelops; Apollo, Cinyras, Zacynthus, Hyacinthus, Phorbas, Hylas, Admetus, Cyparissus, Amyclas, Troilus, Branchus, Atymnius, Parus, Potnieus, and Orpheus; Dionysus, Adonis, Ampelus, Hymenaeus, Hermaphroditus, and Achilles; Asclepius, Hippolytus; Hephaestus, Peleus; Pan, Daphnis; Hermes, Perseus, Chrysus, Thersus, and Odrysus; and Heracles, Abderus, Dryops, Iocastus, Philoctetes, Ilas, Polyphemus, Haemon, Diomus, and Pirithous.

lexical_decisions.source_quote: πάντων μετὰ Διὸς θεῶν ἀφθόνους εὑρήσεις κοινωνίας
lexical_decisions.rationale: The source separates this adjective and noun with the verb. The adjective can mean abundant or free from jealousy and grudging; the argument against jealousy supports ungrudging, while abundant unions is a material alternative.

The stated erotic love supplies the understood verb for the ensuing series of gods and their named male beloveds. The English preserves every listed person and does not add ages or acts beyond the source.

This name in Apollo's list begins with upsilon and a rough breathing. It is distinguished in transliteration from the printed Ἴλα in Heracles' list rather than silently treating the two spellings as identical.
The printed iota spelling in Heracles' list is retained as Ilas. Identification with the Hylas in Apollo's list is possible but is not imposed on the source text.
